title: Honey on the letters
hook: a medieval custom: children licked honey from letters on their first day of learning

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was upsherin, and your line was three years: the scissors going around the room, and a child who now begins to be taught. What milestone did you mark? Today, the first lesson itself. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight.

A small slate, with the Hebrew alphabet written across it. Alef, bet, gimel, all the way through. Someone has spread honey over every letter. A boy, small enough that he was carried in, sits in front of it beside his teacher. The teacher points to the first letter and says its name, and the boy repeats it. Then the teacher tells him to lick the honey off the letter. He does. Next letter, next lick. His face is sticky, and he's grinning, and the grown-ups in the doorway are grinning too. That is how the custom pictures a child's very first day of learning. Today's line is why.
screen: `A SLATE OF LETTERS.` → `HONEY ON EVERY ONE.` → `SAY IT, THEN TASTE IT.`

segments.voice: Honey on the letters. An old custom for a child's first day of Torah study. Turn it four ways. First, how it went. In the versions old Jewish books describe, a child was wrapped in a prayer shawl and carried to the teacher, so that even the walk felt set apart. Letters were written on a slate and covered in honey to lick off, and some versions add cakes and eggs with verses written on them, eaten after the lesson. Details vary from telling to telling. The heart doesn't: the first taste of learning is sweet. Second, the prophet who ate a scroll. In Ezekiel, the prophet is handed a scroll and told to eat it. He does, and in the old Jewish Publication Society translation he says: "it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness." Words, taken in so completely they become food. And they taste of honey. Third, the Psalms. Psalm nineteen describes God's teachings as more precious than gold and sweeter than honey from the comb. The custom takes that line at its word. If Torah is sweeter than honey, then start with honey, and let the child find out the rest is sweeter still. Fourth, today. Some Jewish schools and families still put a drop of honey on a letter card when a child begins to read Hebrew. A grown-up doesn't need a slate. But the question carries: what would it take for the next thing you learn to taste sweet, not like a chore?
screen: `CARRIED TO THE TEACHER.` · `A SCROLL THAT TASTED OF HONEY.` · `SWEETER THAN THE HONEYCOMB.` · `A DROP ON A LETTER CARD.` · then, large: `LEARNING IS SWEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: taste honey while reading. If you have honey, or anything sweet, put a little on your fingertip or your tongue. If you don't, imagine it. Settle, and breathe. Now take one line you'd like to learn: a verse, a poem, a sentence from a book on your shelf. Read it slowly, once, while the sweetness is still there. Then close your eyes and say it back. If it slips, read it again. No rush. Let the taste and the words arrive together. The bell holds the time.
Honey on the letters. A child's first lesson, licked off a slate, because the words were meant to taste sweet from the start. Today's word.

Your line: learning is sweet. Today, pair something you're learning with something you enjoy, a good drink, a favorite chair, and notice if it goes in easier. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Some Jewish schools and families mark a child's first Hebrew lesson by putting honey on letters for the child to taste, echoing an old custom for the first day of Torah study.

notes: Ezekiel 3:3 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording.
Psalm 19:11 paraphrased ('more precious than gold, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb'). The script says 'Psalm nineteen' (Jewish verse numbering 19:11; KJV 19:10).

The index calls this 'a medieval custom'. Under the claims rule the script says only 'an old custom' that 'old Jewish books describe'. The usual sources are Machzor Vitry and Sefer HaRokeach (Ashkenaz, 11th–13th c.), which describe the tallit, the honey slate, and cakes and eggs with verses. Present-day practice phrased as 'some Jewish schools and families'; confirm.
